text:
Education in **Australia** is a state and territory-managed system, with the federal government playing a supporting role in funding and regulation. Compulsory education spans from **pre-primary (kindergarten, ages 4–6)** to **Year 12 (ages 17–18)** , covering primary (Years 1–6) and secondary (Years 7–12) schooling. The **Australian Curriculum** sets national standards, while each state/territory administers its own education system, including curriculum delivery, school governance, and funding.
Primary schools focus on foundational literacy, numeracy, and social skills, while secondary schools offer specialized subjects, culminating in the **Senior Secondary Certificate of Education** . The system is divided into **government schools** (64% of students), **Catholic schools** (19.7%), and **independent schools** (16.3%). Schooling is free in government schools, though many charge voluntary fees for materials and activities. The **National Assessment Program – Literacy and Numeracy (NAPLAN)** assesses student progress annually in reading, writing, language, and numeracy.
Australia’s tertiary education is largely public, with universities and vocational education institutions (TAFE) offering degrees and diplomas. International students form a significant portion of tertiary education, contributing to Australia’s education export industry. The country ranks highly in global education indices, though challenges include **funding disparities** , **teacher shortages** , and **achievement gaps** among Indigenous students. The **Gonski Review** (2012) aimed to address funding inequities, though implementation has been slow.
